cards.body: Economist Paul Krugman says AI is a technology for the very rich: huge spending, very few jobs. Writer Noah Smith says the gains already reach ordinary people, in four ways.

sections.text:
Jobs: construction jobs have grown since the AI boom began in late 2022. Builders' pay has also risen faster than average pay this year.

Taxes: data centers (big buildings full of AI computers) pay property and sales taxes. Loudoun County in Virginia, the world's biggest data center hub, uses this money for top schools, libraries and new roads.

Growth: Trump's tariffs and policy chaos should have cut spending and growth. Data center building pushed spending up.

Users: people get far more value from chatbots than they pay. Economists call this extra value "consumer surplus".

sections.label: The numbers
items: $172 billion a year: the consumer surplus from AI in the US (Brynjolfsson and co-authors, April 2026). That is more than OpenAI's and Anthropic's yearly revenue combined.
500,000: new construction and trades jobs Goldman Sachs says data center building will need by 2030.
About 1 million: Americans who would lose work if growth fell by just 1 percentage point, by Okun's Law (a rule of thumb linking growth to jobs).
One third: the share of a data center's cost that goes on construction. Krugman uses this to argue the job gains are small.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Smith does not call AI harmless. He names real costs: strain on the power grid, noise, possible job losses later, and people leaning on AI until their thinking gets weaker. His point is narrower: the claim that the gains skip ordinary people does not fit the data. Towns can also ask more of data centers, like cheaper power and water, and money for schools and parks.

recall.q: Krugman says AI does almost nothing for ordinary Americans. What four kinds of benefit does Smith point to instead?
recall.a: Construction jobs and faster-rising builders' pay; data center taxes that pay for local schools, libraries and roads; data center spending that kept the economy going despite Trump's tariffs and policy chaos; and about $172 billion a year in value for chatbot users beyond what they pay.

cards.title: Siberian lab worker dies of plague; nearly 200 isolated
cards.body: A lab worker in Irkutsk, Siberia, has died of plague. She reportedly broke a test tube of live bacteria. Nearly 200 people she may have met are now isolated. None are sick so far.

sections.text:
She was 27 or 28 and worked at the city's anti-plague institute. Media reports say she told doctors she broke the tube while collecting samples. She went into hospital on Tuesday with severe pneumonia (a serious lung infection). She was put on a ventilator and died on Thursday.

Reports say it was pneumonic plague. This form attacks the lungs. It spreads between people through tiny droplets when they cough or breathe. Officials have not confirmed which form it was.

Her hospital is under quarantine. Irkutsk has cancelled public events. Police have opened a criminal case over possible safety failures. The regional governor says all contacts have no symptoms and test negative. He did not mention her death. The head of nearby Buryatia confirmed it.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 197 or more people in medical isolation
More than 100 of them in hospital wards
2 days from hospital to death

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: This plague did not come from nature. Reports say it came from an accident inside a lab built to study the disease. The lung form can pass from person to person. That is why so many people were isolated so fast.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Whether any of the 197 contacts get sick. What the special commission says about the quarantined hospital. Where the criminal case goes.

recall.q: How did the lab worker reportedly catch plague, and why were nearly 200 people isolated?
recall.a: She reportedly broke a test tube of live plague bacteria while collecting samples. Reports say it was pneumonic plague, which attacks the lungs and spreads between people through droplets. So officials isolated everyone who may have been near her. So far, all of them test negative.
